## Bretonnia and the Wasteland

## **The Bretonnian Coast**
Despite its many perils, for the coastal communities scattered about the coasts of Bretonnia the Sea of Claws is life. 

Fishermen depart before dawn every morning, returning after dark with holds laden with catch. Merchant ships depart for distant ports, coming back brimming with rich cargoes. Smugglers slip into quiet coves or the docks of friendly villages. Wreckers lure the foolish onto hidden reefs. Pirates stalk the coast, looking for vulnerable prey while avoiding the attention of the Bretonnian Navy. 

The merchant rulers of L’Anguille and Marienburg struggle to control the trade routes crisscrossing the Sea of Claws, a centuries-old rivalry that occasionally manifests in violence out on the waves. The Sea of Claws can be deadly and unforgiving, but for those willing to brave it, fortune awaits. 

The Bretonnians have long claimed to be the greatest sailors in the Old World. Certainly, their fleet is something to behold, each magnificent galleon bristling with cannon and decorated with beautiful murals and sculptures. Most Bretonnian nobles have little interest in maritime matters, and as a result most naval vessels are crewed by commoners. A life at sea is one of the few ways a peasant can rise beyond the limitations of Bretonnia’s restrictive class system. 

Most Bretonnian seafolk, of course, never serve aboard a warship. Instead, they brave the seas in humble fishing skiffs or merchant cogs. It is in such vulnerable vessels that the Bretonnian reputation for seamanship is earned. The coast of the Sea of Claws is harsh and unwelcoming, requiring skilled sailors to navigate safely. The Great Lighthouse beckons ships to L’Anguille, the only port of note on Bretonnia’s northern coast. 

## **’ the Dragon S Maw**
To the north and west of the Gulf of L’Anguille lies the Dragon’s Maw. Any sailor with a semblance of sanity refuses to go anywhere near the region, as it has a deadly (and well-deserved) reputation. Sharp rocks rise from the water like jagged teeth, wreathed in the spray of the vicious tides that constantly hammer their sides. The currents are unpredictable, visibility is poor, and to make matters worse the area is subject to frequent storms. The coast is so inhospitable that it is almost entirely uninhabited. The local lord has offered a handsome reward to anyone able to map a safe route through the Maw, but so far no one has been foolish enough to take him up on the offer. 

The Sea Elves claim that Silenna Starguided, a famed navigator, once charted a way through the Maw. Charlatans sometimes try to sell fake copies of her charts in L’Anguille, though rarely for very long. L’Anguille has lost too many sons and daughters to the Maw to take such scams lightly, and con artists trying to pass off dangerous forgeries tend to be thrown in the harbour. 

Rumour has it that the Maw is considered a holy site by cultists of Stromfels. Some cultists whisper that there’s a temple at the heart of the Maw, filled with treasures. Others claim that it’s just a tale to draw in the greedy; more sacrifices for the Shark God. 

Only a very foolhardy captain would seek to navigate through the Dragon’s Maw. See page 104 for **Making Progress** . The rocks of the Maw count as having a Collision Rating of 60 (see page 111). In addition, any boat taking 20 Wounds or more from a collision with one of the rocks in the Maw suffers _Holed_ 1 (see page 117). 

## In the Dragon’s Mouth
As they pass the Maw, the Characters spot a sailor floating in the water, clinging to some wreckage. He’s the only survivor of a ship that was wrecked on the Maw’s treacherous rocks. Sure enough, the Characters soon catch sight of a cog caught on a reef at the edge of the Maw. Its hull is torn open, and it’ll clearly never sail again, but the survivor claims he could lead a party of rowboats over to retrieve its valuable cargo. 

## **The Marches of Couronne**
The stark coastline of Couronne is sparsely inhabited. The region is regularly beset by storms, and there are no locations suitable for a deep harbour. Every coastal village is fortified against the frequent raids of Norscans and Dark Elves. There is little to attract legitimate traders to the area, and the locals tend to be wary of visitors. 

The marcher lords have little interest in the coastal region, being more concerned with their horses and their feuds, leaving the locals to fend for themselves. The only assistance the commoners of Couronne can hope to receive is from the Bretonnian Navy, but even their ships are viewed with suspicion. Naval patrols along the coast are usually carried out by buccaneers from L’Anguille — private vessels granted a royal charter to keep the sea lanes open. They are often crewed by captured smugglers, wreckers, and pirates, sentenced to serve aboard ship in lieu of execution. As such, they are often little better than the raiders from whom they supposedly protect the coast. 

Despite this, local fisherfolk often sign up to serve on such ships, hoping to win enough gold in spoils to buy themselves a life in L’Anguille or Marienburg. They are welcomed by buccaneer captains, for they are skilled sailors with expert knowledge of the Couronne coast. 

During times of conflict with Marienburg or the Empire, the king will offer bounties on enemy ships, and every village will be awash with privateers (and their booty). Some buccaneers occasionally engage in a little piracy even in times of peace, tempted by the fat merchant cogs coming to and from Marienburg. 

## Looking a Gift Horse in the Mouth
The Characters have been hired to fetch a cargo from a small fishing village on the coast of Couronne. When they arrive, they discover that the cargo is a dozen prize horses. Wrangling these nervous beasts onboard their ship will be challenging enough, but what to do when a very angry marcher lord arrives (accompanied by a dozen men-at-arms) and demands the return of his property? 

## **L’anguille**
The rugged coastline of the Gulf of L’Anguille is notoriously dangerous. Sheer cliffs, unpredictable currents, and rumours of dangerous creatures preying on the unwary mean that the area is popular only with wreckers, smugglers, and the occasional cultist. But the Great Lighthouse guides ships to safety, leading them to L’Anguille, Bretonnia’s great merchant city. 

L’Anguille was originally the Elven colony of Tor Alessi, and much of the original architecture survives, especially in its infrastructure. The Great Lighthouse towers above everything, its light visible out to the Sea of Claws. 

The walls of L’Anguille stretch from the Lighthouse to surround the city, but the buildings within are all Humanmade, clustered between the walls and the harbour. On an island in the middle of the harbour squats Castle L’Anguille, a Human-built fortification that looks out of place next to the graceful Elven structures. 

The city’s inhabitants are proud seafolk and see every day on the water as a challenge. It’s a rare family that doesn’t have someone out at sea, whether fishing, trading, or serving aboard a Bretonnian warship. Returning safely is an event worth celebrating, and local taverns come to life in the evening as the fishermen bring in their catch. 

Ships of the Bretonnian fleet can almost always be found in L’Anguille, including one or two of the great galleons for which it is famed. Many locals serve on Bretonnian warships, and the fleet is looked upon with favour by the city. Off-duty sailors sometimes cause trouble, but the locals forgive a bit of roughhousing in the dockside inns, as long as everyone can walk away from the encounter. 

Duke Taubert once made his home in the city, but five years ago he moved south to Grasgar Castle, and has not returned since. In his stead, Godemar Fitzgodric serves as his steward. Godemar is the wealthiest merchant in Bretonnia, and head of the Brethren of the Lighthouse, one of the most prestigious merchant clubs in the kingdom. He has great plans for L’Anguille and has already ordered the construction of four new watchtowers to protect the city. 

## **The Great Lighthouse**
The Great Lighthouse towers over the Gulf of L’Anguille, visible for miles in every direction. Standing three hundred feet tall and built from smooth white stone, it makes the neighbouring Human buildings look crude by comparison. The city walls extend from the Lighthouse; sixty feet high and almost as deep, they present a formidable obstacle for any invader. 

Elves often visit the Lighthouse, and it is rumoured that there are secret tunnels and chambers throughout the building that can only be accessed by their kind. 

The Lighthouse is mostly staffed by navy veterans, who are too old (or too injured) to serve at sea. These old mariners are a great source of sea lore and chanties and are always happy to reminisce about their glory days. 

The Great Lighthouse counts as a lighthouse in all respects (see page 108), though its light can be seen from a much greater distance than that of a regular lighthouse.

## A Flickering Flame
As their ship approaches L’Anguille, the Characters notice that the light from the Lighthouse seems to be flickering on and off. It quickly becomes apparent that the changes aren’t random — they’re some kind of coded signal! But who is sending it, and to whom? And what is the message? 

## **The Wasteland**
Stretching from the mouth of the Reik to the Sea of Claws, the Marienburg Sound (or the Manaanspoort Sea, as it is known to Wastelanders) is always bustling with sea traffic. Hundreds of fishing vessels supply Marienburg with their daily catch. Merchant traders bring their wares from near and far. Occasionally an Imperial warship might be spotted, having passed through the city from the Reik, and now making its way to a posting along the Nordland coast. 

Most ships take the slower, but safer, north-eastern passage through the bay, guided by the lighthouse at Fort Solace. This small village is administered by Marienburg’s Wasteland Import-Export Exchange. While ships sometimes stop there for the night, it offers little beyond the most basic of services, as Marienburg’s rulers seek to encourage ships to travel to the city proper. 

Daring (or foolish) ship captains take the more dangerous north-western route through the bay. Rocky shoals line the western shore, and strong currents can sometimes cause a ship to veer off-course. Wreckers have been known to light beacons along the shore to confuse ships. 

## Calculated Risks
A ship taking the north-east route can make an **Average (+20) Boat Handling** Test. Taking the north-western route is **Challenging (+0)** but will reduce the travel time of the journey by a day. However, a failed Test will result in the ship having to negotiate a number of Shallows (see page 112) equal to the number of negative SL generated on the Test. 

Along the western shore lies an ancient, raised road of white blocks, built by the Elves millennia ago. Known as the Old Coast Road, it winds its way from the Grootscher Marshes and along the coast, continuing to Couronne and eventually ending just short of L’Anguille. The years have not been kind, and much of this highway has fallen into the sea or been broken apart by locals looking for construction materials. Tancred Castle is the last seat of a Bretonnian Knight before the territory of the Wasteland. 

Squeezed between the Old Coast Road and the Manaanspoort Sea is the village of Broekwater. A small cluster of fishing hovels, Broekwater has a poor reputation and is said to be a haven for criminals of all sorts. The goods of ships wrecked along the western shore can sometimes be found here. Anyone asking about lost cargoes at the Shark’s Eye (the village’s one inn) will be directed towards Hendrika Baas. This ancient-looking crone can be found mending nets on the shore, and (for a price) can arrange for the delivery of ‘salvaged’ wares. She can also put discreet enquirers in touch with the Marienburg branch of the Fish, the largest smuggling gang at work on and around the Reik. Those who anger Hendrika rarely make it out of Broekwater. Some say that they end up being sacrificed to the sea, with Hendrika herself leading the rites. 

The ruins of Almshoven lie north of Broekwater. This small village and its lighthouse were destroyed by Norscan raiders during the Great War Against Chaos. Wastelanders claim that the Norscans practised dark magics there, and that the place is now cursed. Despite this (or perhaps because of it), the ruins are often used as a hideout for those seeking to escape attention for a while. Adventurers are sometimes drawn to the ruins in search of treasure, and the fact that some don’t return merely adds to the village’s notoriety. 

At the mouth of the bay lies Reaver’s Point. It was once home to a great gathering of pirates and wreckers, until the Great Families of Marienburg assembled an army of mercenaries and ships to destroy them. The tides sometimes uncover pieces of the pirate encampment or wash up bits of old wreckage. Scavengers can sometimes be found here, hoping to find lost pirate treasure, but for the most part the area is only frequented by smugglers. 

At the very north-eastern tip of the Wasteland, on the border of the Laurelorn Forest, is the isolated town of Arnau. Ships stopping here report a quiet settlement of farmers and fisherfolk, with a surprising martial bent. The town militia is well-equipped and drills regularly. Whenever the fog rolls in off the Tumble Downs to the west, Baron van Buuren has the militia muster and stand at the ready. When asked why, locals mutter about ‘oneeyed demons’ and lock their doors. 

## **Marienburg**
Marienburg is the greatest trading city in the Old World (much to the irritation of the merchants of L’Anguille). A stream of ships travels along the Rijksweg, the channel of the Reik which splits the city in half. The enormous Hoogbrug Bridge spans the Rijksweg, so huge that even the tallest of ships can pass beneath it. To either side cluster dozens of islands sat within a maze of canals and bridges, covered in tall buildings that lean over the water. Even the bridges are home to inns, shops, and residences. The industrious and enterprising Marienburgers make use of every inch of space available, and where every inch has already been taken, they simply build up. 

The stereotypical Marienburger is a greedy, fast-talking merchant, who will talk you out of your life savings in exchange for taking all your worldly possessions off your hands. In truth they’re no greedier than anyone else, but the city’s focus on trade means that its citizens are used to haggling over prices and striking a good deal. When they see an opportunity, they take it, and they make no apologies for it. 

In the north of the city is found the Elven enclave of Sith Rionnasc’namishathir (more commonly known as Elftown). Under the terms of the Treaty of Amity and Commerce, Elftown was granted to the kingdom of Ulthuan, and is not subject to the laws or customs of the rest of the city. In exchange, the Merchant Houses of Marienburg gained the exclusive right to act as the Elves’ agents for goods sold in the Old World. The Sea Elves have also helped protect the city from attack, most notably at the Battle of Grootscher Marsh, in which Marienburg secured its independence from the Empire. 

## **City Politics**
Marienburg is, in theory, ruled by the Stadsraad, a two-house parliament consisting of the city’s priests, academics, and a handful of nobles (the upper house), and representatives of the city’s guilds and aldermen (the lower house). In practice the city is ruled by the Executive Council of the Stadsraad, known as the Directorate. True power lies with the heads of the city’s ten wealthiest families (collectively referred to as the Ten), each of whom has a seat on the Directorate. The remaining seats are held by the rector of Baron Henryk’s College and the high priests of the city’s temples. The leader of the Directorate is elected to the position of Staadtholder and is always one of the Ten. 

Competition amongst the Ten is fierce, and the membership has changed over the centuries as family fortunes have waxed and waned. While overt violence between the families is frowned upon, espionage, theft, sabotage, and even a little piracy are tolerated, as long as the peace and prosperity of the city are not threatened. The one thing the Ten agree upon is that the safety and independence of Marienburg must be protected at all costs. An unspoken rule forbids the assassination of fellow Directors, but this does nothing to protect their agents and employees. 

## **Trade**
Trade is the lifeblood of the city, and merchants from across the world can be found here. Kislevite fur-traders rub shoulders with Norscan blade-mongers, next to Arabyan spice merchants or Cathayan silk traders, and currencies from across the world mix with the city’s own coin, the Marienburg Guilder. Locals are used to dealing with foreign coins and are adept at recognising their value. Most will take them at face-value, preferring to secure a deal rather than quibble over exchange rates. 

No tax is levied on river traffic coming through Marienburg, but the city still finds ways to profit. Any ship wishing to enter or leave Marienburg must accept the services of a licensed pilot, at the cost of 1 shilling per yard of ship’s length. Ships inevitably spend at least one night in the city, and docking and unloading fees, patronage of inns and taverns by crews, and purchase of supplies and ship repairs all add up. The real money is made at the Wasteland Import-Export Exchange, where all of Marienburg’s bulk trade takes place. Anyone wishing to buy or sell a cargo in Marienburg must do so at the Exchange, using accredited brokers and paying a 2% tax on all sales. 

## **The Cathedral of Manaan**
The Tempelwijk district of Marienburg is home to many shrines and temples, but none compare to the Cathedral of Manaan. The white limestone walls seem to rise from the water. The roof is topped with three golden bell towers, suggestive of Manaan’s trident. Two knights templar of the Order of the Mariner guard the Cathedral’s doors, which are open day and night. 

Upon entering the Cathedral, a worshipper descends into a vast chamber. Smaller shrines and chapels (where Marienburg’s wealthy pray in comfort) lie to either side, but most ceremonies take place in the main nave. At high tide the nave floods, allowing worshippers to pray in direct communion with Manaan. At the end of the chamber, nine steps rise to the great altar, a single block of stone upon which Marius the Fen Wolf is said to have stood when he founded the city. 

But it is what lies behind the altar that truly draws the eye. Behind a huge, clear pane of glass is an aquarium, filled with hundreds of sea creatures. A gift from the Elves of Ulthuan, its creation is beyond anything Humans can accomplish. Pilgrims from across the Old World travel to see this living testament to Manaan’s kingdom. 

The recently appointed matriarch of the Cult of Manaan, Camille Dauphina, resides in the Cathedral. Until recently, Patriarch Wouter Berkhout headed the Cult, but he resigned from his position a year ago. Berkhout was much respected in Marienburg, and the city is rife with speculation as to why he stepped down. 

Sailors often attend service at the Cathedral before embarking on a voyage, in the hopes of winning Manaan’s favour. The Cathedral is also occasionally used by people of importance when they need to meet discreetly — they ‘just happen’ to attend service at the same time. 

## Eight Limbs Good, Four Limbs Bad
The Cathedral recently purchased a rare breed of octopus for its aquarium, but the beast somehow escaped. The creature is small, agile, poisonous, and surprisingly intelligent. The Cathedral will pay handsomely for its return. Unfortunately, someone else is also looking for the fugitive cephalopod: August Bardolino, master chef at the Prince’s Rest (Marienburg’s most exclusive inn), wants to add it to the menu. 

## **The Brotherhood of Seamen and Pilots**
The guildhall of the Brotherhood of Seamen and Pilots is well known to most sailors who frequent Marienburg. Sitting at the centre of the Suiddock district on the Bruynwater canal, it stands out from the warehouses and taverns to either side. A painted mermaid sits above the pillared facade that fronts the building, and a domed roof is topped with a brass representation of Manaan’s crown. 

Some say the building looks more like a temple to Manaan than a guildhall, and in truth guild members often join in a quick prayer to the Lord of the Seas before a meal in the mess hall or a meeting of guild members. Members often pray at the small chapel to Manaan at the rear of the hall, rather than attend their local temple. 

The guildhall is often frequented by sailors just in from a long journey, who gather to catch up on gossip, swap stories, discuss the working conditions on various ships, and sometimes look for work. The mess hall serves a tasty fish stew, and the guild turns a blind eye to downon-their-luck sailors who spend a night or two bunking under their roof. 

Guildmaster Albert Loodemans is a respected figure in the local community. Known for his calm demeanour and common-sense attitude, he has steered the Brotherhood through Marienburg’s politics for the past five years. One growing irritation, however, is the rival Riverfolk’s Association, led by the ever-aggravating Axel Huurder. 

There has long been bad blood between the Brotherhood and the Association, but lately the Riverfolk have been accusing the Brotherhood of attacking their members or sabotaging their boats. Albert has been trying to calm tempers and improve relations between the two groups, but secretly fears that some of his own guild may be stoking tensions. 

## Blood in the Water
Prominent members of the Brotherhood have gone missing. Everyone suspects the Riverfolk’s Association, but an Elven blade was found at the scene of the latest disappearance. Someone is being framed, but is it the Association, the inhabitants of Elftown, or both? 

## **Baron Henryk’s College**
Established in 1947 IC, Marienburg’s premier institution of learning is one of the most renowned centres of education in the Old World. Located in a former palace in the Tempelwijk district, the College’s musty halls are always bustling with academics, students, and their longsuffering servants. The surrounding streets and plazas hold tea-houses, inns, taverns, and boarding houses, where wealthy young students and scholars can be found debating esoteric topics, getting drunk, or drunkenly debating esoteric topics. 

Study at Baron Henryk’s is open to anyone who can afford the fees. In addition to the standard three-year curriculum required to earn one’s Magister Philosophiae Naturalis, the College also engages in advanced studies in medicine, law, and ‘economicks’ (a new science promoted by the Temple of Haendryk). However it is in the study of navigation and cartography that Baron Henryk’s truly excels. In addition to teaching practical navigation skills, the College has sponsored many expeditions to distant lands, and the Cartography Department now has one of the greatest map collections in the Old World. 

The College is also known for its ‘Department of the Maritime Arts Magical’. Rumoured to have existed in some form before Teclis brought the gift of magic to the Empire, officially it was created in 2310 IC, as an ‘adjunct campus’ of the Altdorf Colleges of Magic. Though Marienburg is now independent, the Department is still technically under the purview of the Altdorf Colleges. Students from Altdorf sometimes take a semester in Marienburg to study maritime magics, and students from Baron Henryk’s often travel to Altdorf to finish their studies. Though lacking the breadth of magical knowledge found in Altdorf ’s Colleges or Middenheim’s Guild of Wizards, Baron Henryk’s provides instruction in sea magics unknown elsewhere in the Old World. 

## The Dreamer’s Journal
Someone has stolen a centuries-old tome from the College library, and Professor Gert-Jan Kikkert desperately needs the services of a ship to pursue them into the Sea of Claws. The professor insists that they must catch their quarry before they reach the Dragon’s Maw, though he is rather cagey as to why. Oddly enough, soon after leaving Marienburg, the Characters notice that an Imperial warship seems to be following them. 

## **Sea Magics**
The Department of the Maritime Arts Magical warns apprentices that the Winds of Magic gather and flow in strange ways on the seas. Some Winds are harder to control, while others flow in overwhelming surges. Baron Henryk’s is also known to teach spells particularly suited to life at sea not widely known beyond Marienburg. 

The following modifiers apply to channelling or casting attempts while at sea: 

**Lore of Beasts:** _Ghur_ sinks below the waves, where it sits amongst the great beasts of the abyss. Amber wizards can draw upon this power, but it doesn’t like to be disturbed, and may lash out. Spells from this Lore Critical or Fumble on both doubles and rolls divisible by 10. 

**Lore of Fire:** _Aqshy_ is hard to summon at sea. Channelling Tests for this Lore suffer from –1 SL. However, if a ship _Aqshy Aqshy_ on is on fire, floods towards it. Channelling a ship currently ablaze benefits from +1 SL (in addition to the normal benefits from _Ablaze_ Conditions applied to the Lore of Fire). This may explain why Bright Wizards have a terrible reputation amongst mariners. 

**Lore of Heavens:** During stormy weather _Azyr_ crashes down from the skies, and almost seems to want to be directed by a wizard’s will. When the seas are calm, however, _Azyr_ stubbornly refuses to be called, fighting any efforts to bend it into a spell. Lore of Heavens spells cast during a storm benefit from +1 SL to Casting Tests. Spells cast when becalmed suffer –1 SL to Casting Tests. 

**Lore of Life:** _Ghyran_ saturates the seas, granting a Jade Wizard easy power. However, _Ghyran_ ebbs and flows, and a wizard can lose control in an instant. SLs from Channelling Tests are doubled on the seas, but a Critical Channelling results in a Major Miscast rather than a Minor Miscast. If you have the _Aethyric Attunement_ Talent, roll on the Minor Miscast Table instead. 

## **Lore of Life**
The Druids of the Jade School may seem out of place aboard ship, but their presence is much welcomed by savvy captains. _Ghyran_ flows through the seas, making a Jade Wizard a valuable addition to any crew.

A crew can be ordered to cut the ship free with an **Extended Challenging (+0) Boat Handling** Test, to a target number equal to the caster’s Willpower Bonus + SLs.

You gather _Ghyran_ from the sea, taking small amounts of water with it. Cleansed of impurities, this water flows to the ship’s stores, replenishing any empty barrels of water. 

## **Lore of Heavens**
Celestial Wizards often seem aloof and bookish to the crew of a ship, but some have come to love life at sea. On the open ocean an Astromancer can commune with _Azyr_ in ways unheard of on land. They often climb to the crow’s nest to contemplate their arts, tracing the twists and turns of the Blue Wind with their fingers. 

## **Blessings of Bel Shanaar**
## **Cn:** 2
## **Range:** You
## **Target:** Self
## **Duration:** 1 Day
This spell must be cast while on a journey with a set destination, the location of which is known to the caster. Closing your eyes, you focus your Second Sight on the heavens, tracing _Azyr’s_ path as it crackles across the sky, seeming to jump from star to star. For an instant a bolt of _Azyr_ connects you to your destination, leaving a shimmering blue afterimage in your vision. For the duration of the spell, all Navigation Tests made by the wizard (or involving the wizard, in the case of Crew Tests) benefit from +2 SL.

**Target:** One ship

## **Whirlpool**
## **Cn:** 6
**Range:** Willpower yards × 10 

**Target:** AoE (Willpower yards) 

**Duration:** Willpower Bonus Rounds 

You pull on the _Ghyran_ surrounding the target area, moving it around and around. The water starts to churn, and a whirlpool forms in the target area. Whirlpools are described on page 114. The spell creates an area of Gentle Rotation, but SL can be spent on making the whirlpool larger as per the Overcasting rules. 

This spell is a variation of one created by Lord Astromancer Wilfried-Gotthelm Niezlib, who sought to use it to prove his theories about the movement of celestial objects. He later realised it had more practical applications, and modified it to determine the exact moment a ship should fire a broadside. The caster can calculate the roll of the ship, distance to the target, weight of the cannonballs, and the power of each shot. For the duration of the spell, Tests made to fire a cannon benefit from +1 SL.

## **Elves Upon the Sea of Claws**
The Sea of Claws is not known as an area of great interest to the Elves, though they are active there. 

Ulthuan sends trading missions to Marienburg. There is growing competition between the merchants of Lothern and those of Cothique to reach new markets and exploit the opportunities they present. Elftown in Marienburg is home to delegations from both kingdoms, and whilst they provide a united front to the eyes of their Human neighbours, they privately engage in intricate schemes to undermine one another, or find loopholes in their treaties with their human agents in Marienburg. 

The Loremasters of Saphery also have an interest in Marienburg. They desire to keep a close eye on developments in Altdorf, where the Colleges of Magic are found. These institutions have taught relatively safe principles of wizardry laid down by Teclis over two centuries ago, but as far as many Elves are concerned, they amount to nothing more than a risky ongoing experiment. 

Wary of angering the Human wizards (who are more numerous, if not so powerful, as their own mages) the Loremasters of Saphery send missions to tutor and spy upon them. The independence of Marienburg, and the 

fact that it contains its own magical college, is a worry to the Loremasters. They would prefer their journeys to Altdorf to be as frictionless as possible, so that any information they collect from Altdorf does not come into the possession of their enemies or rivals, and that the magic taught at Baron Henryk’s College remains true to the principles laid down by High Loremaster Teclis. 

## **Intriguing Situations**
This is a potential source of conflict between the Elf Kingdoms, as Lothern and Cothique enjoy the rich trading opportunities afforded by Marienburg’s liberal attitudes and laws, which have flowered because of its independence. On the other hand. there are many in Saphery who would find it comforting to see Marienburg come under the control of the Empire once again. 

The Sea of Claws provides a route to the Great Ocean, the island of Albion, the land of Ulthuan, and the continent of Lustria. These lands are rich in secrets and treasures that the Elves of Ulthuan would rather remain hidden from the eyes and hands of Humans. Whilst privileged traders are permitted to berth at ports such as Lothern and Tor Koruali, their presence there is tolerated rather than welcomed. The seas about Ulthuan are patrolled by the High Elf navies, whose Dragonships are swift and crewed by peerless sailors. 

## **The Sea Lord Aislinn**
The Lothern Sea Guard are the most skilled naval fighting force in the world, captained by the Sea Lord Aislinn. He is a controversial figure in Lothern society, dubbed ‘the Pernicious’ even by those who have cause to thank him for their security upon the waves. He shows a relish for bloodshed that unnerves his fellow High Elves, taking savage delight in the opportunity to engage an enemy upon the waves, or lead hit and run shore raids against Norscan settlements. 

Proud, with a pronounced cruel streak, any Human or Dwarf who treats him with disrespect is likely to be challenged to a duel, and he has a particular (and peculiar) loathing of Halflings. 

## **The Dark Elves**
Yet Ulthuan faces such perils that there is a need to promote the likes of Sea Lord Aislinn. Without his navies the eastern shores of Ulthuan would be a soft target for the Norse, and the High Elves would be an open target for the vengeful Dark Elves of Naggaroth. 

The Dark Elves are sailors every bit as skilled as their counterparts from Ulthuan, and they are in possession of several Black Arks. These vessels combine aspects of both battleship and fortress. They were created during the Sundering, when the northern marches of Ulthuan were shattered and drowned during the titanic conflict that saw the Dark Elves banished to the freezing wastes of Naggaroth. 

The towers of several sorcerers were spared from this calamity as enchantments were woven into them, keeping them integral and buoyant. Rather than sinking beneath the waves, they broke free of the ground and became massive floating fortresses. 

## **Black Arks**
The Black Arks enable the Dark Elves to project massive power far from their home shores, for each vessel is so large that it can garrison armies of corsairs, house massive beasts of war, and provide the laboratories and libraries of Dark Elf Sorcerers, all at once. 

Since the secession of Marienburg, the Empire have been inhibited from protecting their shores, but still the Dark Elves take care when sailing the area, desperate not to lose another of their precious Black Arks. 

## **A Task for Khyrathi Bayne**
Instead, they are hatching a plan to appeal to the Elves of the Laurelorn to assist them in their vengeance. The Witch King has deemed it appropriate to send an agent, the assassin-corsair Khyrathi Bayne, to spy upon the denizens of the Laurelorn, and come up with a strategy that will lead to greater cooperation between Naggaroth and the Eonir. 

Khyrathi is more interested in bloodshed than diplomacy, but she is a patient Elf and has some confidence that, should she succeed in her current mission, the Witch King will find her future work more in line with her tastes. She believes a potential area of common interest could be the Humans of Nordland. 

If she can sow discord between them and the Elves, perhaps Queen Marrisith might take the first steps in fostering an alliance with the Dark Elves. 

The loss of a Black Ark is a sore blow to the forces of Naggaroth, and two have met with stiff resistence in the Sea of Claws. _Ecstasy of Pain_ was badly damaged after being caught between Bretonnian corsairs and a Nordlander navy, and part of its ramparts now makes up a tower of Castle Salzenmund. _Cleaver of Souls_ was wholly destroyed by a punitive expedition led by Admiral Burnetz of Ostland, though she lost her life, alongside her whole fleet, in the effort to sink the Dark Elf vessel. 

The Dark Elves are not quick to forget such humiliations, but they are also wary of suffering further defeats. Whilst they raid villages along the shorelines of the sea, they are careful not to attract the attention of Bretonnian or Imperial warships.
